newsitem.title: USA: Amid renewed Fed fears, few buying U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Amid renewed Fed fears, few buying U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Up until last Friday morning, it seemed as if investors in U.S. Treasury securities were willing to buy at any price.

Now, dealers are having trouble practically giving the stuff away. That's evidenced by a more than four-point freefall in the market even after the notes and bonds sold this week "cheapened up" substantially.

What happened in the past eight days, analysts said, was a major shift in market psychology. That led to, in the words of Goldman Sachs & Co Inc money market economist John Youngdahl, "a pretty severe break in the technical environment."

Indeed, from its high of 116-31/32 just over a week ago, with visions of 122, the September bond contract plunged to 112-21/32 by Friday's close -- breaking through key support levels few thought possible, including 114-12/32 (6.50 on the 30-year bond) and then its 50-day average of 112-29/32.
Analysts predict that after penetrating yet another support level at 112-24/32, the September bond is poised to retest the 110-23/32 low seen on June 20.

Similarly, the bond's yield currently stands above 6.60 percent, a level not seen since before the July 4 holiday. Just last Thursday, the bond had reached a 1-1/2-year low of below 6.30 percent. Many were predicting a long bond of 6.25 percent heading to 6.0 percent, but now, 6.75 percent seems the next stop.

"Until last Friday, the market was under pressure to rise almost continuously. It was an irresistable force. People were trapped into positions that never made economic and market sense," Youngdahl said. As a result, "This has been a dramatic correction."

He and others believe that a test of 6.75 percent is likely, thanks to a couple of strong economic reports and a trio of Treasury quarterly refunding auctions. With hindsight, traders characterized the auctions as "pretty lousy" since retail customers just do not appear willing to want to own Treasury securities when the Federal Reserve may soon have to raise interest rates again.

Most of the damage was done at the long end, as the 30-year at 6.64 percent was trading some 20 basis points above its auction level. Meanwhile the 10-year note, at 6.37 percent, was changing hands at 17 basis points higher than where it was auctioned. The three-year note was up only 10 basis points at 6.14 percent from 6.04 percent.

"The Street was getting comfortable with the concept of no Fed tightening," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at UBS Securities LLC. "There was some glimmer of hope that the next move in the future would be an ease. That was quashed with last week's data."
Both the employment report and National Association of Purchasing Management reports for July were much stronger than expected and reignited fears of inflation.
Thus, "The refunding could not have come at a worse time with respect to the change in (market) thinking," Dimick said. "We are having a serious case of indigestion trying to distribute the paper."
Since the market viewed the economy as nirvana with many putting on mostly long positions and curve steepening trades, the strong data caught most players off guard.
Treasuries look to take a breather over the next few sessions and stick to narrow ranges until Wednesday's July retail sales data, which were seen dictating near-term price action, dealers said.

But although the consensus called for a 0.5 percent rise in sales, many economists have raised estimates for a gain of 0.8 to 1.0 percent. Such increases were in the process of spooking the market into thinking that real growth would be stronger than anticipated in the third quarter.

"We might well test the high end (of yields)," Youngdahl said. "It is going to take a surprising or shocking (weak) economic environment to provoke people into a buying mode in the next three, four weeks."
